lesson.menu_title: If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.menu_desc: Everyday decisions that hang on something else -- the sky, the forecast, a plan that might fall through -- with the first conditional -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 12 -- If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.grammar_point: first conditional for real future possibilities (if + present simple, will/might)

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: To cancel something that was already arranged
With very little warning before something happens
To fail before it happens, after it was already arranged
A statement about what the weather is probably going to do
It is very likely that something will happen
A second plan you keep ready in case the first one fails
A short period of very heavy rain
To find time for something in a day that is already full

vocab.text: Notice the pair: you call something off, but a plan falls through on its own. One has somebody deciding; the other simply happens to you.

reading.rtitle: The Fair That Happens Rain or Shine
paras: On the second Saturday of every month, the square in Serra Verde fills up with old furniture, seedlings and coffee. Nobody sells anything expensive. People bring what they have restored during the month, and everything depends on one thing: the sky. "If the forecast is good on Friday, we put out forty tables," says Dona Marta, who has organized the fair for eleven years. "If it looks bad, we put out twenty and we keep the rest in the shed."

The rule is painted on a board next to the church door, and it has not changed since 2014. If it rains before eight in the morning, everything moves into the old school gym. If the rain starts after that, the sellers cover their tables and carry on. The fair is never called off and it is never postponed. "People drive an hour to get here," Dona Marta says. "If we cancel one Saturday, half of them will not come back for three months. That is the part nobody thinks about."

Last March the town found out how well the plan works. A downpour started at twenty past seven, and by eight o'clock the gym was full of tables, seedlings and wet dogs. Not a single seller went home. "You cannot count on the weather out here, so you count on the backup plan instead," says Tiago, who restores chairs and has had a table since the first year. "If you wait for a perfect Saturday, you will wait forever. Chances are it will rain on the good ones too."

reading.prompt: What is the best title for this text?
choices: How bad weather closed a small town market
A monthly fair that plans for rain instead of hoping against it
Why restored furniture sells better in the countryside

items: The number of tables depends on the forecast on Friday.
If the forecast is good on Friday they put out forty tables; if it looks bad, only twenty.
If it rains at ten in the morning, the fair moves into the gym.
Only rain before eight moves the fair inside. After that the sellers cover their tables and carry on.
The fair has been called off on a few rainy Saturdays.
The text says the fair is never called off and never postponed.
In March the sellers stayed even though a downpour started.
Not a single seller went home. By eight the gym was full of tables, seedlings and wet dogs.

items.situation: A friend asks what you are doing this weekend. You do not know yet, because it depends on the sky. Answer in three sentences.
tips: If it is dry on Saturday, I will work outside.
If it rains, I will stay in the workshop.
Chances are I will do a bit of both.

items.situation: Somebody invites you to a fair two hours away, on short notice, and the forecast is bad. Say what you will do and on what condition.
tips: I will go as long as the road is fine.
If there is a downpour, I will call it off.
I will let you know on Friday night.

items.situation: A neighbor says he will help you carry a heavy table on Sunday, but he is not sure yet. Ask him about it and offer a backup plan.
tips: If you cannot make it, tell me on Saturday.
If it falls through, I will ask somebody else.
Unless it rains, we will do it in the morning.

items.situation: You have four things to do this weekend and time for three. Say which one you will postpone, and what has to happen for you to squeeze it in.
tips: If I finish early on Saturday, I will squeeze in the painting.
If I run out of time, I will postpone it.
It is up to me, and the dogs always come first.

answerkey.title: Reveal the rule in one page
list: First conditional = a real possibility in the future. If + present simple, then will + verb: "If it rains, we will move inside."
The future lives in ONE half of the sentence only. Never put will after if: "If it will rain" is wrong.
You can start with either half. The comma appears only when the if half comes first: "We will move inside if it rains."
will can become might or may when you are less sure: "If the forecast changes, I might stay home."
unless already means if not, so it never takes a second negative: "Unless it rains", never "unless it does not rain".
as long as and provided that add a condition you insist on: "I will go as long as the road is fine."
when = you are sure it happens; if = you are not: "When I get there" against "If I get there".
Expressions: a forecast, a downpour, to call off, to postpone, a backup plan, to fall through, to squeeze in, on short notice, to count on, to run out of, chances are, to be up to you.

listenings.text: Good evening, this is the recorded message for the Serra Verde fair. If you are calling about Saturday, here is everything you need to know. The forecast is not good, but the fair is going ahead. If it is raining before eight in the morning, we will set up inside the old school gym, and there will be a sign on the church door telling you where to go. If the rain starts later than that, we stay in the square and everybody covers their own table, so bring plastic. If you are a seller and you cannot make it, please call this number tonight, because if you do not tell us, we will hold your table until eleven and somebody else will lose the space. One last thing. If you are driving in from the main road, take the second entrance and not the first one. Chances are the first one will be flooded again.

People think that living out here means having endless free time, and it does not work like that at all. My whole weekend is a set of conditions. If I wake up and the sky is clear, I will be outside by seven, because the good light does not last. If it is raining, I will move into the workshop and do the sanding, which I can do in any weather. If a friend calls on short notice and says she is passing through, everything else gets postponed, and I do not feel bad about that anymore. The only rule I really keep is that if I run out of energy by four in the afternoon, I stop. I used to push through and then lose the whole of Sunday. So now, if the day is going badly, I will call it off early and start again the next morning. It sounds like a small thing, and it changed everything.

extra_audio.text: First, Tiago asks Ana whether she is taking a table at the fair on Saturday. Then Ana says that she will decide on Friday, when she sees the forecast. Next, Tiago reminds her that the fair is never called off, whatever the sky does. After that, Ana admits that her real problem is the varnish, which needs two dry days. Finally, Tiago offers her half of his own table if her pieces are not ready in time.
